newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Telekom rivals file new complaints.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Telekom rivals file new complaints.

text.p: Encouraged by the recent success of regulatory challenges against Deutsche Telekom AG, two of the phone giant's rivals filed fresh complaints that, if successful, could further pave the way for competition.

Telekom's two main domestic rivals, Mannesmann Arcor AG and O.Tel.O, filed complaints with the Post and Telecommunications Ministry in Bonn, urging the government to intervene in negotiations over prices for network access.

The companies have been in talks with Telekom for months over how much it will cost them to access the monopoly's local phone networks in order to provide services to their own customers when markets open to competition on January 1, 1998.

Called interconnection by the industry, such agreements form the basis for new competitors when a telecommunications market opens, because in most cases new companies do not have sufficient networks of their own.
Mannesmann and O.Tel.O charge that Telekom is demanding prices that are not in line with its costs and that would make it difficult for them to offer competitive services.
"The conditions in the offer from Telekom are not cost-oriented," a Mannesman Arcor spokeswoman said.

The complaint comes a week after the Post and Telecommunications Ministry ordered Telekom to provide rivals with an offer by July 14 that would enable them to connect to its monopoly network in so-called unbundled interconnection.
This means rivals would be able to connect to the access lines of residential and business customers without leasing any switching services from Telekom.
The new complaint is the first over interconnection prices.
The ministry confirmed it had received the complaints and said it now had up to 10 weeks to make a decision on the specific charges.

Interconnection charges in most cases are the largest single cost factor for telecoms companies entering a new market and as such will have significant bearing on whether the new services can be provided profitably.
The government regulator now has two options in trying to determine fair interconnection prices.

The first would be for the ministry to gather data from Deutsche Telekom and make a determination of the costs to the company for providing access to its local networks. But ministry have indicated this would be very difficult to do.

A more likely approach is for the ministry to determine a fair interconnection price based on "comparable markets", using information from other European markets and, possibly, from the United States.

A spokesman for O.Tel.O, jointly owned by utilities RWE AG and Veba AG, said it had not yet received a specific price offer from Telekom, but that Telekom had indicated a price of around six pfennigs per minute.
That is significantly higher than interconnection prices in Britain or the United States, where markets have been open to competition for years, and also above the two pfennig level set by France.
"Deutsche Telekom is playing for time," a spokesman from O.Tel.O said.
